name: Jötnar

pitch_detail.notes: Approach pitch; moderate free climbing to establish first belay on the wall
130 feet; easy free climbing up small ramp to left, steep cracks to large ledge, then thin aid on face to stance below splitter crack
80 feet; splitter cracks to sheltered slabby belay; excellent portaledge bivy site
120 feet; crux aid pitch - A3 up left-facing crack with roof halfway up, hook doom block, exit corner right past hooks to stance below mud corner
Varied climbing with water seepage risk; afternoon waterfall conditions common
Continued aid climbing with water seepage; often running water in spring/early summer
130 feet; left-facing corner on rivets to steep crack series overhanging 40+ feet; fixed line recommended for descent
150 feet; A2 from belay, C1 up beautiful splitter hand crack through overhang (5.10), 5.9 free climbing to belay - classic pitch
140 feet; second aid crux - right of bush quest on thin pins, rivets, hooks; bat hooks bypass chossy corner; long reach to beaks near top at bolt (tension traverse or reach)
Mixed climbing transitioning to upper wall pitches
Continued aid with improving rock quality
Easier aid climbing as route approaches summit section
Further aid climbing with reducing difficulty
Upper pitches include traverse left to large right-facing corner with 5.10 or C1 root aiding, and a 5.7 mossy dihedral and gully to summit - deteriorating rock quality near finish

rappel_detail.notes: First rappel from the top; plan on at least two ropes given the sustained overhanging terrain.
hazards: the wall overhangs enough on many pitches that the next station is not below you - plan on swinging in or leaving directional gear on nearly every rappel, and expect a free hang if you miss

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 2 of 16, one per pitch, from the bolted anchor at the top of pitch 15.
Rappel 3 of 16, one per pitch, from the bolted anchor at the top of pitch 14.
Rappel 4 of 16, one per pitch, from the bolted anchor at the top of pitch 13.
Rappel 5 of 16, one per pitch, from the bolted anchor at the top of pitch 12.
Rappel 6 of 16, one per pitch, from the bolted anchor at the top of pitch 11.
Covers the pitch that overhangs 40+ feet; this section requires either fixed lines or down-aiding to manage the roof.
hazards: the biggest overhang on the route - rappelling it clean without a fixed line strands you off the wall
rappel_detail.station: This is the pitch that overhangs 40-plus feet. Without a line fixed on the way up you have to down-aid a long way to stay on the wall and reach the next station; a 40 m line is reported to be long enough to fix here.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 8 of 16, one per pitch, from the bolted anchor at the top of pitch 9.
Roughly the midpoint of the wall; the FA party's long haul-bag-rider rappel spanned part of this middle section.
Rappel 10 of 16, one per pitch, from the bolted anchor at the top of pitch 7.
Rappel 11 of 16, one per pitch, from the bolted anchor at the top of pitch 6.
Rappel 12 of 16, one per pitch, from the bolted anchor at the top of pitch 5.
Rappel 13 of 16, one per pitch, from the bolted anchor at the top of pitch 4.
Rappel 14 of 16, one per pitch, from the bolted anchor at the top of pitch 3.

hazards: arriving at the gear belay and looking for bolts that are not there is the trap on this station
rappel_detail.station: Pitch 15 is the one pitch without a bolted belay - the belay is gear, on a large ledge. The bolted rappel anchor is set far to the right along that ledge as you face the wall, not at the belay, so walk the ledge to find it.

rappel_detail.pull: Strip any lines fixed during the ascent on the way down; leaving them is discouraged here and the buttress already carries old rope from previous attempts that should not be trusted.
rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel to the base; remove any fixed lines left during the ascent as an established leave-no-trace practice on this route.

rappels: Rappel the route (~16 raps from bolted anchors on all pitches but P15); much of the wall overhangs, so many rappels swing significantly or need a directional piece left to reach the next station cleanly; expect to down-aid a long section of P7 if no fixed line was left in place
descent_text: The descent is accomplished by rappelling the route in full. Due to the sustained overhanging terrain throughout most pitches, careful anchor placement is critical, particularly on pitches with significant roofs. Climbers should plan to use at least two ropes for rappelling. The first ascent team used an unconventional technique where one climber managed haul bags on a very long rappel before the remaining climbers rappelled in pairs off stainless steel anchors. Plan to remove fixed lines during descent to preserve the rock.
approach: From the Lake Serene Trailhead, hike Trail #1068 about 4 miles and 2,000 ft of gain to Lake Serene, then follow the unofficial path around the right-hand (west) side of the lake and traverse talus and huge boulders toward its south end below the Middle Peak (Jötunheim) massif. This cirque holds the Norwegian Buttresses, home to big-wall routes like Jötnar, one of the tallest walls in the Lower 48; reaching the base involves further talus and brush travel beyond the lake. Given the technical, multi-day nature of routes here, most parties approach with overnight gear.
overview: Jötnar is the most sustained aid route in Washington State, ascending the left side of Mount Index's North Norwegian Buttress via a continuous crack system located approximately 100 yards left of the Doorish line. The route features 2,000 feet of mixed free and aid climbing across 16 pitches on granite with strong alpine ambiance.
beta: This is the only repeatable Grade VI big wall in the Pacific Northwest with bolted stainless steel anchors and portaledge bivy opportunities achievable by experienced wall climbers in 3-4 days. Climbing follows a continuous crack system featuring varied aid pitches including thin pins, rivets, hooks, and roof passages. The Fang Roof (Pitch 8) stands out as a classic pitch with hand crack free climbing through an overhang. Plan for 7 days of capsule-style climbing with portaledge camps to complete the first ascent.
gear: Double rack of nuts and cams (micronuts to #4 Camalot, single #5)
10 rivet hangers (including #1 size for deep rivets)
2 sets of hooks (bat hooks and other variants)
Portaledge (required; no natural ledges exist on route)
Portaledge fly and rain shell (afternoon seepage common)
fa: Sam Boyce, Lani Chapko, Kyle Willis, 2020 (reconnaissance trip June 2020; completed capsule-style on a send push of roughly 7 days of climbing, late July-August 2020)
